fatal_errors: The proposed compositional substitution does not reconstruct the target intervention of cold rolling followed by controlled recovery/recrystallization annealing.
The claim that Nb substitution will preserve yield strength near 1719 MPa is not directly supported by the cited evidence.
The intervention is compositionally ambiguous: replacing 10–20% of the Mo inventory is very different from replacing 10–20 at.% of the whole alloy.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the requested strength–plasticity problem and offers a testable compositional alternative, but it diverges substantially from the hidden paper. The target used a low-Mo, Nb-rich Nb35Zr26Ti19Hf15Mo5 alloy and altered its microstructure through 20–80% cold rolling and 650–800 °C annealing. Its operative mediators were dislocation accumulation, low-/medium-angle boundaries, texture, recovery, and partial recrystallization—not reduced electronegativity mismatch through Nb-for-Mo substitution. Consequently, the predicted processing trends, tensile conditions, and quantitative outcomes are not recovered. The cited six-component subtraction study provides some directional rationale for elemental effects, but it does not establish that the proposed substitution in NbZrTiHfMo will retain a yield strength near 1719 MPa. The proposed composition series, common processing, phase checks, and explicit strength-loss threshold make the falsification experiment reasonably discriminating, although TEM/EBSD or direct measurements of dislocation mobility and chemical short-range order would better test the asserted mechanism.
